newsitem.title: UK: Oil steady as focus switches from war to winter.
newsitem.headline: Oil steady as focus switches from war to winter.

text.p: World oil prices were slightly higher on Monday when concerns about shortages of heating oil in the approach to winter took over as the market's main preoccupation after the threat of hostilities in the Gulf eased.
Benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude oil futures for November delivery closed 27 cents up at $22.27 a barrel on 1534 GMT on London's International Petroleum Exchange.

Traders said evidence of reduced tension in the oil-rich Gulf came on Sunday with news that the United States may remove one of its aircraft carriers from the region because Iraq appeared to be backing away from a confrontation with Washington.

World crude prices rallied to a post-Gulf War high of $24.39 a barrel 10 days ago after the United States fired cruise missiles at Iraqi targets in retaliation for Baghdad's decisive intervention in Kurdish factional fighting.

Gas oil -- used for heating oil and diesel -- showed no sign of giving up recent gains, however, and some traders and analysts said prices could revisit recent five-year highs of $227 a tonne as consumers rush to fill tanks ahead of winter.
"This market is demand driven and it's going to be heating oil that pushes it higher," said another trader.
October gas oil closed $4.00 up at $218.25 a tonne.

"Gas oil demand is likely to be strong in the near term because of low stocks in Germany...and because the U.S. market will inevitably call on European refiners to meet at least a part of the additional demand in the coming months," said finance house Kleinwort Benson in a report.

Tight heating oil stocks in the Atlantic basin are forcing Europe and the United States to compete for supplies. Stocks in the U.S. East Coast -- the biggest heating oil market in the world -- are running 19 million barrels below year-ago levels.
"We're likely to be open to some very big spikes if we see some very cold weather coming in," said a trader.
The possibility of an early resumption of Iraqi crude exports bringing relief to refiners running flat out to rebuild stocks also appeared to recede further over the weekend.

In an interview with Reuters late on Friday, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said he did not know if the oil-for-food plan for Iraq would be implemented next month or before the end of the year.
"We still have difficulties to implement this," he said.
Boutros-Ghali put the May 20 deal on hold after Iraqi troops entered the Kurdish-inhabited northern region of Iraq, delaying the deployment of U.N. personnel to monitor aid distribution.

The sustained strength in prices -- Brent is still nearly $5 a barrel more expensive than this time last year -- is bringing windfall revenues to OPEC despite overproduction by several of the group's members
OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman and OPEC President Rakad bin Salem bid Rakad met in London on Sunday ahead of the cartel's quota compliance meeting on September 25.

The committee meeting in Vienna will compare official and independent assessments of the group's output but OPEC sources say little will be done to deal with overproduction with oil prices remaining relatively strong.
Analysts say the group is producing 800,000 barrels per day (bpd) above its agreed supply quota of 25.03 million bpd.
